cohort: Pregnant women between 37 and 42 weeks of gestation, with uterine inertia and prolonged labor as the indication for cesarean section, were included in the study.
finding: Extraperitoneal cesarean section (EXPCS) was associated with statistically significantly lower levels of infection markers (leukocytes, CRP, fever), less postoperative pain (lower tramadol + metamizole and diclofenac usage, lower VAS scores), and potentially fewer intraperitoneal adhesions compared to transperitoneal cesarean section (TPCS).
mod_finding: Extraperitoneal cesarean section (EXPCS) was found to reduce postoperative infection, pain, and potentially adhesion formation compared to transperitoneal cesarean section (TPCS).
followup_time: 3 days post-delivery (for infection markers) with some follow-up for adhesions at an unspecified later time if subsequent surgeries occurred.
